    Supernatant Phase in Polyelectrolyte Complex Coacervation: Cluster Formation, Binodal, and Nucleation

    Abstract

    This work studies the structure and thermodynamics of the supernatant phase in polyelectrolyte complex coacervation, a relatively unexplored area. By combining the cluster theory in dilute solution with our recently developed mean-field theory for inhomogeneous polyelectrolyte solutions (Zhang, P.; Wang, Z.-G. Macromolecules 2021, 54, 10994), we systematically investigate the structure of finite-sized clusters formed by oppositely charged polyions in symmetric dilute solutions and how these clusters affect the binodal, spinodal, and nucleation for polyelectrolyte complex coacervation. We find that both the polyion concentration deep inside the cluster and the interfacial tension decrease with increasing the cluster size, reaching their respective bulk coexistence values with corrections inversely proportional to the cluster radius. The polyion concentration in the supernatant phase at coexistence is several orders of magnitude higher than that obtained under the uniform mixing approximation. For most relevant conditions away from the critical point, the supernatant phase consists predominantly of polyion pairs. By examining the nucleation barrier in supersaturated solutions, we can determine a pseudo-spinodal when the barrier is a few multiples of the thermal energy. The location of this pseudo-spinodal is similarly shifted to much higher concentrations than predicted under the uniform mixing approximation. Making the volume approximation for the clusters, we obtain simple analytical expressions for the cluster formation free energy, the modified binodal, and the pseudo-spinodal. In particular, we propose a simple approximate formula for estimating the concentration of the coexisting supernatant phase in terms of the chain length, interfacial tension, and the polyion concentration in the coacervate phase.

      I. Introduction

      ARTICLE SECTIONS
      Jump To
      Polyelectrolyte complex coacervates formed via an associative liquid–liquid phase separation by mixing oppositely charged polyelectrolyte (PE) solutions have a broad range of industrial applications, such as polymer film fabrication, hydrogel formation, and protein encapsulation. (1−15) In protein therapeutics, for example, protein drugs can be encapsulated in the polypeptide complex coacervate droplets for effective and efficient drug delivery and subsequent release. (5,8,13) Polyelectrolyte complex coacervates also have significant biological relevance due to their role in bioinspired adhesives, membraneless organelles, and artificial protocells. (6,16−27) In recent years, considerable efforts have been devoted to understanding the structure and dynamics of polyelectrolyte complex coacervates, and significant progress has been made on both the theoretical and experimental fronts; (28−84) we refer the readers to several recent excellent reviews. (85−93)
      In contrast to the coacervate phase, conspicuously less attention has been paid to the supernatant phase with which the PE-rich coacervate is in equilibrium. While the supernatant phase is too deficient of PEs to be of practical use, studying the structure and properties of this phase is still important for several reasons. First, varying the parameters in the supernatant phase provides a convenient and effective way to modulate the physical properties of the coexisting coacervates. For example, increasing the salt concentration in the supernatant phase in general results in swelling of the coacervate and thus a decrease in the storage modulus. (38,91,94) Second, quantitative and accurate determination of polymer concentration in the supernatant phase is an integral part of understanding the phase behavior of PE complex coacervation. For example, in cell biology, the saturation concentration that represents the polymer-poor branch of the binodal serves as a key physical quantity to characterize the minimum amount of proteins for forming a membraneless organelle. (21,22) Finally, examination of the structure, energetics, and distribution of the clusters in the supernatant phase can provide valuable insights into the phase-transition kinetics in solutions of both synthetic and biological polyelectrolyte systems, i.e., whether phase separation proceeds via nucleation and growth or spinodal decomposition. (95−97)
      Due to the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged polyions, polycations and polyanions in the supernatant phase are expected to form finite-sized polyion pairs or clusters, as first pointed out by Veis and co-workers in the 1960s. (86,98) However, most of the theoretical investigations, such as the Voorn–Overbeek theory, (2,37) random phase approximation, (29,30,34,40) transition matrix theory, (44) and liquid-state theory, (54) assume that the polyions, small ions, and solvents are uniformly mixed, and do not account for these finite-sized PE clusters in the supernatant phase. These theories thus cannot properly describe the structure and thermodynamics of the supernatant phase. The situation is similar to uncharged homopolymer solutions, where the Flory–Huggins theory, which ignores the collapse of the polymers in poor solvents, predicts exponentially low monomer concentrations in the degree of polymerization for the polymer-poor branch of the binodal, (99) whereas a modified theory that accounts for the globule/clusters (100−105) yields monomer concentrations that are many orders of magnitude higher than that predicted from the Flory–Huggins theory. (104,106)
      By combining the random phase approximation and the Lifshitz–Grosberg theory of polymer globules, (100,107) Borue and Erukhimovich first examined the equilibrium structure of a symmetric neutral globule formed from one polycation chain and one polyanion chain, under the so-called volume approximation that is valid for a sufficiently large globule. (108) Subsequent work by Rumyantsev and Potemkin suggested that, in the absence of small ions, such neutral globules can form even when the polyion concentration is far below the supernatant binodal, i.e., when the solution is undersaturated with polyions. (42) Based on the premise that all polycations and polyanions form neutral globules, Tainaka argued that polyelectrolyte complex coacervation results from the condensation of these globules due to electrostatic correlation (109−111) based on a virial expansion approach, while Adhikari et al. attributed the driving force for coacervation to the combined effect of dipolar and hydrophobic interactions. (50) Field-theoretical simulation by Delaney and Fredrickson clearly demonstrates that, for complex coacervation in the absence of small ions, oppositely charged polyions exist in the form of chain pairs and the polymer concentration in the supernatant phase is orders of magnitude higher than that predicted by the random phase approximation. (43) In systems with asymmetric polycation/polyanion chain length or concentration, the clusters can adopt more complex structures such as tadpoles (112) or cylinders/lamellae, (113) in addition to simpler spherical globules. Moreover, a series of computer simulation studies have been performed to examine the complexation behavior between oppositely charged polyions, and these studies show that the duplex formed by a pair of symmetric oppositely charged polyions roughly adopt a spherical structure. (114−120)
      In spite of these progresses, a systematic study on the cluster structure and energetics in the supernatant phase and how incorporation of the clusters affects the phase boundary and phase separation kinetics is lacking. In this work, we conduct such a study for the simplest symmetric coacervates where the clusters are expected to be electrically neutral and spherical. By generalizing our recently developed mean-field theory for inhomogeneous polyelectrolyte solutions, (82) we first examine the structure, interfacial tension, and formation free energy of finite-sized clusters comprising equal numbers of polycations and polyanions. The formation free energy is then used to determine the cluster size distribution and the concentration of the coexisting supernatant phase. Our results show that away from the critical point, the clusters are predominantly in the form of single polyion pairs. The polyion concentration in the coexisting supernatant phase is shown to be several orders of magnitude higher than predicted from the uniform mixing approximation. We further use the cluster size distribution in the supersaturated state to calculate the free energy barrier for nucleation, from which we determine a pseudo-spinodal where the free energy barrier becomes order of the thermal energy. In Section II, we present the model and the general theoretical framework for calculating the cluster properties. The results are presented and discussed in Section III, where we first consider the salt-free system and then examine the effects of added salts. We conclude with a brief summary along with some outlook.

      II. Model and Theoretical Framework

      ARTICLE SECTIONS
      Jump To
      We consider a symmetric mixture of strongly charged polycations and polyanions in solution, with each polyion consisting of N coarse-grained monomers. For simplicity, we assume the counterions of the polyions to be the same as the salt ions, and all monomers, ions, and solvents to have the same volume v. Generalization to account for the size disparity among different species is straightforward. We further assume that all polyions are fully charged and both the monomers and salt ions are monovalent. Under appropriate conditions, the solution undergoes a liquid–liquid phase separation into a polymer-deficient supernatant phase and a liquid coacervate phase which contains most of the polymers. As alluded to in the Introduction, oppositely charged polyions are expected to form finite-sized clusters due to the electrostatic attraction─provided the polyion concentration is not too low and the salt concentration is not high─an effect that is not accounted for in most theoretical studies of the coacervation phase behavior. For symmetric mixtures, the clusters are expected to be electrically neutral, containing equal numbers of polycations and polyanions and equal numbers of small cations and anions. Unlike in ref (42), where the free energy was constructed based on a reference state of unpaired polycations and polyanions, we assume all chains are in the form of electrically neutral clusters and there are no unpaired polyions. We denote the cluster size by the number of polycations (or polyanions) m; thus, an m-cluster contains m polycations and m polyanions. For the concentration range of interest in this work, the number density of these clusters, i.e., the number of m-clusters per unit volume, cm, is sufficiently low and inter-cluster interactions can be safely ignored. Thus, the system can be considered a dilute solution of these clusters. Let Wm be the free energy of an m-cluster, the total free energy of a system with the cluster number density cm in a total volume is

      The Lagrange multiplier μp in eq 2 is naturally interpreted as the chemical potential of the polyions in the cluster on a per-monomer basis. For undersaturated solutions, μp is determined by the total polyion concentration in the system. However, at the coexistence with the coacervate phase, μp must equal the chemical potential of the coacervate phase, which in turn determines the concentration of the polyions in the supernatant phase.
      The free energy of the cluster, Wm, is the key quantity in determining the cluster size distribution and other thermodynamic properties of the supernatant phase. Computer simulation (115,117) of the complexation of a single polycation and a single polyanion showed that the two chains in a polyion pair form a well-mixed “scrambled eggs” structure (122) as a spherical globule. We expect this to be true for any m. We thus consider a single m-cluster centered in a spherical volume of sufficiently large size containing the polyions with the small ions and solvent. Since the small ions and solvents in a cluster are in equilibrium with the outer reservoir, the volume is a semi-open system─open with respect to small ions and solvent but closed with respect to the polyions. The free energy of the cluster Wm is the excess semi-grand potential, i.e., the semi-grand potential minus the grand potential of the reservoir without the polyions.
      We apply the inhomogeneous mean-field theory developed in ref (82) to this spherical volume of a semi-open system containing an m-cluster. For a symmetric mixture with radial density profiles of polycations (or polyanions) and cations (or anions) given, respectively, by ϕp(r) and ϕs(r), connected to a reservoir with cation (or anion) chemical potential μs, corresponding to a cation (or anion) concentration ϕs,r, (123) the semi-grand free energy functional reads

The three terms in the first line account for the mixing entropy of polyions, small ions, and solvents, and the last term is the generalized Debye–Hückel correlation free energy (124) for disconnected ions with diameter σ ≡ v1/3. We note that some authors excluded the polymer contribution in the mixing entropy (100,108,125) on the ground that the center of mass is fixed for the cluster; here, we include this contribution so as to reproduce the bulk phase for a sufficiently large cluster. The difference between these two approaches is numerically inconsequential for large N. The fourth term is a first-order approximation for the chain connectivity contribution to the electrostatic correlation, where we have made a further simplification by dropping an O(N–1) term; we refer interested readers to the detailed derivation in ref (82). The electrostatic correlations embodied by the last two terms in eq 5 provide the driving force for phase separation. The second term in eq 4 is the well-known Lifshitz conformation entropy penalty due to inhomogeneous polymer density, (107,126) where b is the Kuhn length of the polymer.
      In this work, we focus on symmetric mixtures, for which the average local charge density is zero everywhere and there is no mean-field electrostatic contribution to Jm. For general asymmetric mixtures, there can be charge separation in the interfacial region and then Jm will include a mean-field electrostatic contribution; see ref (82) for details. Moreover, here we focus on the simplest model for polyelectrolyte complex coacervation, which includes only the electrostatic correlation, the chain connectivity, and excluded volume effects (accounted for by incompressibility); we ignore any χ interactions among polymers, solvents, and salt. Incorporation of these interactions will clearly lead to richer and more complex phenomena. However, a systematic investigation on the interplay between the electrostatic correlation and these χ interactions is beyond the scope of this work and deserves a separate study in future.

      It is natural to regard an infinitely large cluster as the bulk coacervate phase. Thus, the polyion concentration ϕp,c and salt-ion concentration ϕs,c in the core of an infinitely large cluster can be considered the equilibrium coexisting concentrations ϕpII and ϕsII of the coacervate phase. (129) These phase equilibrium conditions under the volume approximation for symmetric complex coacervation were first proposed by Borue and Erukhimovich (108) and later used by Rumyantsev, Zhulina, and Borisov. (51) (As mentioned earlier, there is a slight difference between our current theoretical formulation and that in refs (108) and (51) regarding the polyion contribution to the mixing entropy: our fb in eqs 16 and 17 includes this contribution, while refs (108) and (51) excluded it. Both approaches can be justified: ignoring this term is reasonable from the point of view of a polyion pair or small clusters, while keeping it allows the large cluster to be treated consistently as a bulk phase. Since the contribution from this term to the osmotic pressure is rather small for large N, we do not consider this difference important.) For the salt-free case, ϕs,r = ϕsII = 0, and thus, ϕpII can be determined simply by solving Π(ϕpII) = 0.
      From eq 17, λp,∞ is the chemical potential of the polyions in the coacervate phase μpII. By equating this chemical potential with the chemical potential in eq 2, we determine the cluster size distribution ϕm at the coexistence. The polyion concentration on the supernatant binodal is then ϕpI = ∑m=1 ϕm.

      III. Results and Discussion

      ARTICLE SECTIONS
      Jump To
      In our model system, complex coacervation is driven by the electrostatic correlation whose strength is characterized by lB/σ. For an aqueous solution at room temperature, lB ≈ 0.714 nm. When taking into account the temperature dependence of the dielectric constant of a pure solvent ϵr, lB increases with temperature and thus our theory can capture the lower critical solution temperature behavior of complex coacervation. (61,83) However, for the purpose of this work, we do not pursue this explicit temperature dependence; instead, we regulate the electrostatic correlation strength by varying lB/σ, which can be achieved experimentally by varying the temperature, solvent type, or the segment size. In this section, we first examine the symmetric solution without small ions. After calculating the structure and formation free energy for clusters consisting of different pairs of polyions, we construct the cluster-corrected binodal and spinodal curves in the ϕp–lB/σ plane. To understand the numerical results, we perform simplified analysis of the formation free energy, supernatant binodal, and nucleation, based on the volume approximation for the polyion pair. We then examine how the addition of small ions affects the cluster structure and the corresponding formation free energy, and how the incorporation of clusters affects the binodal and spinodal in the polymer–salt concentration (i.e., ϕp–ϕs) phase diagram. In the numerical calculations, we set N = 100 and b = σ.

      III.I. Salt-Free Case

      III.I.I. Structure and Interfacial Tension of Finite-Sized Clusters

      We start with examining the structure and interfacial tension of the finite-sized clusters formed in a dilute solution of symmetric mixtures of polycations and polyanions in the absence of small ions. In Figure 1a, we show the radial polycation (polyanion) concentration profile ϕp(r) for clusters consisting of m = 1, 10, and 50 polyion pairs, respectively, for lB/σ = 1.785 (corresponding to σ = 0.4 nm). In all cases, ϕp(r) consists approximately of an inner uniform core and an outer diffusive surface layer where ϕp(r) decreases rapidly toward zero. Note that the polycation concentration in the uniform core is simply ϕp,c, as defined by the reference state when calculating the interfacial tension. With increasing m, ϕp,c decreases gradually and approaches ϕpII in the limit of m → ∞. Moreover, the surface layer for the different m-clusters is located approximately at the same r/m1/3b. Finally, we remark that the cluster structure obtained in our work─with a nearly uniform core separated by an interfacial region─is markedly different from the Gaussian density distribution assumed by Tainaka. (109−111)
      As a quantitative characterization for the m-dependence of ϕp,c, Figure 1b shows that ϕp,c = ϕpII(1 + Cpm–1/3) for large m, where Cp > 0 is a constant that increases with decreasing lB/σ. This m-dependence is a reflection of the Laplace pressure effect (cf. eq 15) since the osmotic pressure inside a finite-sized droplet is higher than that of the infinitely large cluster (which in turn equals that of the surrounding reservoir) and the difference is inversely proportional to the radius of the droplet. (127,130) To maintain a higher osmotic pressure for a smaller cluster, a larger polymer concentration ϕp,c is required.
      The behavior of ϕp(r) for clusters at other values of lB/σ is qualitatively similar. Quantitatively, with decreasing lB/σ, the core density ϕp,c decreases and the interfacial layer becomes more diffusive; see Figure S1a for details. These phenomena are expected due to the weakening of electrostatic correlation with decreasing lB/σ.
      Figure 2a,b shows, respectively, the locations of the surface of tension R* and the interfacial tension γm for the clusters. At a given lB/σ, R* is nearly proportional to m1/3, i.e., R* ≈ CRm1/3, where the coefficient CR is larger for smaller lB/σ, consistent with the decreased density at decreased electrostatic correlation. On the other hand, γm is larger for smaller m and γm ≈ γ∞ (1 + m–1/3Cγ), where γ∞ ≡ limm→∞ γm and Cγ > 0 is a constant. By invoking the relation R* ∝ m1/3, we then obtain γm ≈ γ∞ (1 – 2lT/R*), where lT is the Tolman length (128,131) that characterizes the curvature correction. From Figure 1b, we see that lT < 0 and its magnitude |lT| increases with decreasing lB/σ.

      III.I.II. Formation Free Energy of Clusters, Binodal, and Spinodal

      The free energy of formation ΔWm ≡ Wm – mW1 in eq 3 is the free energy change between an m-cluster and m polyion pairs (without the translational entropy of the clusters) and is the driving force for coalescing m polyion pairs into a single m-cluster. When ΔWm is sufficiently negative to overcome the contribution due to the translational entropy of polyion pairs, large clusters will form spontaneously; otherwise, polyions will exist in the form of small polyion pairs. In Figure 3a, we present ΔWm for three representative lB/σ. At each lB/σ, ΔW is approximately proportional to m at large m. Moreover, at a given m, |ΔWm| is larger for higher lB/σ because of the stronger electrostatic correlation and hence the larger interfacial tension.
      As explained in Section II, at a given lB/σ, the polyion concentration in the coacervate phase ϕpII is determined by Π(ϕpII) = 0. From ϕpII, we calculate μp in this phase by eq S1. Along with Wm, we can calculate the concentration of polyions ϕm for the different clusters and then determine the polycation concentration in the supernatant binodal as ϕpI = ∑mϕm. The lB/σ dependence of μp and W1 is given in Figure S1b. In Figure 3b, we show ϕm for clusters with m = 1, 2, and 3, and the total polyion concentration in the supernatant phase ϕpI, as functions of lB/σ. For the range of lB/σ values examined, the overall polyion concentration in the supernatant phase is dominated by the single polyion pairs (i.e., m = 1), as seen by the overlap between the black solid curve and the red dashed curve. For all m, ϕm decreases with increasing lB/σ, indicating that the polyion concentration in clusters in the supernatant phase at coexistence becomes more dilute for larger lB/σ.
      By collecting ϕpII and ϕpI at different values of lB/σ, we construct the binodal in the ϕp–lB/σ plane, as shown by the red solid curve in Figure 4a. At sufficiently low lB/σ, the ion concentration profile in the clusters becomes rather diffusive and different clusters may start to interact with each other as their numbers become more numerous. In addition, long-range critical fluctuation becomes significant near the critical point, the description of which requires advanced techniques such as renormalization group theory. (132) Such a pursuit is beyond the scope of this work. Nevertheless, for completing the phase diagram, in Figure 4a, we qualitatively sketch the missing part of the binodal close to the critical point by the red dotted curve, by visual continuation of the two branches of the red solid curve. For comparison, in Figure 4a, we include the binodal obtained under the uniform mixing approximation (the black dashed-dotted curve), calculated by solving the phase equilibrium condition (i.e., the equality of the polymer chemical potential and osmotic pressure in the two coexisting phases, respectively) from the bulk free energy density given by eq 5. We see that the coacervate branch (i.e., ϕpII) from both methods is nearly the same. However, the supernatant branch (i.e., ϕpI) accounting for the clusters is many orders of magnitude larger than that from the uniform mixing approximation, and the difference is more drastic at larger lB/σ. These features are qualitatively consistent with the field-theoretical simulation study by Delaney and Fredrickson. (43) Moreover, while we are unable to accurately locate the critical point in the cluster model, from the general trend of the supernatant binodal, we expect the critical point to shift to larger lB/σ relative to the prediction from the uniform mixing approximation (the black open circle in Figure 4a).
      At a given lB/σ, when the polycation concentration ϕp exceeds the supernatant binodal ϕpI, a homogeneous solution becomes supersaturated and phase separation is expected to occur via the nucleation and growth mechanism. Assuming that there is no significant barrier in the fusion of clusters, we can calculate the nucleation barrier by examining the free energy landscape using the cluster size (i.e., m) as the reaction coordinate. The size of the cluster at the maximum, denoted by m* hereafter, corresponds to the critical nucleus size. Taking lB/σ = 1.785 as an example, in Figure 4b, we then show our numerical results on the formation free energy of the cluster ΔG as a function of m at several representative values of supersaturation ϕ1 > ϕpI ≈ 1.39 × 10–8. We see that, with increasing ϕ1, both the formation free energy barrier ΔG* and the critical nucleus size m* decreases. When the free energy barrier becomes comparable to the thermal energy kBT, the metastable homogeneous state becomes no longer kinetically viable and phase separation will proceed spontaneously via spinodal decomposition. While a rigorous criterion to distinguish the nucleation and growth regime and the spinodal decomposition regime is lacking, we choose an operational criterion ΔG* = 10kBT, following previous practices for homopolymer solutions (104) and polymer blends, (133−136) to define the effective metastability limit or pseudo-spinodal. Hereafter, we term the special value of ϕ1 at which ΔG* = 10kBT as the pseudo-spinodal concentration ϕps.
      The blue dashed curve in Figure 4a shows the pseudo-spinodal curve so-constructed in the ϕp–lB/σ plane. For comparison, we also include the spinodal under the uniform mixing approximation (the green dotted curve), calculated by the condition ∂2fb(ϕp)/∂ϕp2 = 0. We see that, at a given lB/σ, the pseudo-spinodal calculated from the cluster model is also several orders of magnitude larger than that from the uniform mixing approximation; however, the difference is less drastic than for the binodal. We note that for uncharged homopolymer solutions, the pseudo-spinodal concentration on the dilute side is actually lower than the mean-field spinodal predicted by the uniform (random) mixing (i.e., Flory–Huggins) approximation, (106) which indicates a fundamental difference between these two systems.

      III.I.III. Approximate Analysis of the Formation Free Energy, Binodal, and Nucleation

      To help understand our numerical results and to provide simple analytical expressions, here we perform an analysis of ΔW as well as its implications on the supernatant binodal and nucleation properties, based on the volume approximation of the properties of the clusters. First, using our definition of the surface of tension, we can write the free energy as Wm = wc(ϕp,c)Vm + 2mNμp(ϕp,c) + γmAm with Vm = 4πR*3/3 and Am = 4πR*2 being the volume and surface area of the reference system of the m-cluster, respectively. Under the volume approximation, the density of the core is approximately that of the bulk coacervate phase, i.e., ϕp,c = mN/Vm ≈ ϕpII, and we ignore the curvature correction in the interfacial tension by setting γm ≈ γ∞. The grand potential density at polyion density ϕpII is wc(ϕpII) = fb(ϕpII) – 2ϕpII μp(ϕpII). By invoking (4π/3)R*3ϕpII ≈ mNv, we then have R* ≈ CRm1/3 with CR ≡ (3Nv/4πϕpII)1/3, and Wm = (4π/3) CR3fb(ϕpII)m + 4πCR2γ∞m2/3; thus
      (18)
      Clearly, ΔWm < 0 for m > 1 and ΔWm ∝ m at large m, qualitatively consistent with our numerical results in Figure 3a. Further, the form of ΔWm suggests that the reduction of the interfacial area is the main driving force for the coalescence of small clusters into larger clusters and eventually into a macroscopic coacervate phase.
      From ΔWm and eq 3, we further obtain ΔGm ≈ (−kBT ln ϕ1 – 4πCR2 γ∞)m + 4πCR2γ∞m2/3. When the coefficient of the linear term is positive, formation of clusters with size m > 1 is unfavorable, and the system is undersaturated with the polyions existing in pairs (i.e., m = 1); when the coefficient is negative, the system favors a macroscopically large cluster (i.e., m → ∞). Thus, the vanishing of this coefficient in this analysis provides an estimate of the concentration of polyion pairs at the coexistence. At this condition, ΔGm ≈ 4πCR2γ∞m2/3 = – kBTm2/3 ln ϕ1. Substituting it into eq 3, we obtain ϕm ≈ ϕ1m2/3. This simple relation suggests that the concentration of polyions in clusters with large m, ϕm, is much smaller than ϕ1, and thus, the supernatant phase is dominated by simple polyion pairs (i.e., m = 1), as shown by our numerical data in Figure 3b. Therefore, ϕ1 at this condition is essentially the polyion concentration in the supernatant phase at coexistence ϕpI and we thus have
      (19)
      This relation suggests a convenient estimate of the supernatant binodal ϕpI via ϕpII and γ∞, the latter being more easily and accurately measurable in experiments. The magenta dashed-dotted curve in Figure 4a shows that this analytical binodal can indeed reasonably describe the numerical supernatant binodal (i.e., the red solid curve in Figure 4a). The discrepancy between the two curves is most likely due to neglecting the curvature corrections in ϕp,c and γm when deriving the analytical expression of ΔWm. In addition, a more complete analysis using the equality of the chemical potential will introduce a prefactor involving the concentration of the coacervate. Thus, eq 19 is more suitably viewed as an order-of-magnitude estimate rather than a quantitative one.
      The formation free energy ΔGm also provides valuable insights into the nucleation and growth mechanism when the solution is supersaturated, i.e., when ϕ1/ϕpI > 1. After extremization of ΔG with respect to m, we obtain m* = 2S0/(lnS)3, where S ≡ ϕ1/ϕpI is the supersaturation, and the parameter S0 ≡ (16π/3)N2(γ∞v2/3/kBT)3(ϕpII)−2. The free energy barrier is then
      (20)
      This is the nucleation barrier from the classical nucleation theory, which is valid when the supersaturation is not too high; the validity of the classical nucleation theory has recently been reported for multicomponent biomolecular condensates. (97)
      Note that S0 is proportional to the square of chain length and the cube of surface tension and inversely proportional to the square of ϕpII. These dependences are the same as for uncharged homopolymer solutions. (104) Furthermore, setting ΔG* = 10kBT, we arrive at an analytical approximation of the pseudo-spinodal, i.e.,
      (21)
      Figure 4a shows that this analytical expression provides a reasonable approximation (orange dashed-dotted curve) for the numerical pseudo-spinodal (the blue dashed curve).
      We remark that most of the analysis given in this subsection for the salt-free system carries through to the system with salt. Furthermore, the main results are derived without resorting to specific coacervation theories, so they should be quite general.

      III.II. Effects of Salt Concentration

      Our discussion on the effects of salt ions parallels the discussion on the salt-free system, but here we will only present the numerical results. We first examine the structure and interfacial tension of the m-clusters and then study how incorporation of the clusters affects the binodal and spinodal in the polymer–salt concentration (i.e., ϕp–ϕs) plane. Since the effects of lB/σ have already been discussed for the case without small ions and the qualitative effects remain similar, in this section, we take a fixed lB/σ = 1.785 to focus on the salt concentration effects.

      III.II.I. Structure and Interfacial Tension of Finite-Sized Clusters

      Figure 5a shows the concentration profile of polycation (polyanion) ϕp(r) for clusters with different m when the salt concentration in the reservoir ϕs,r = 0.04. Similar to the case without small ions (i.e., Figure 1a), ϕp(r) for all m also has a uniform core with ϕp(r) = ϕp,c and an outer diffusive surface layer. Likewise, ϕp,c is higher for smaller m due to the Laplace pressure effect. Quantitative comparison between Figures 5a and 1a suggests that the addition of salt leads to a decrease in ϕp,c and a thickening of the surface layer.
      In Figure 5b, we show the cation (anion) concentration ϕs(r) as a function of the scaled radial distance r/m1/3b for clusters with different m. Note that ϕs(r) in the uniform core of the cluster is the same as the concentration ϕs,c defined by the reference state. We see that ϕs,c in the cluster core is in general less than the salt concentration in the reservoir ϕs,r, qualitatively consistent with the bulk salt partitioning behavior reported in our previous work. (53,54,82) Since the structure inside the uniform core of the cluster resembles that of the bulk coacervate phase, the reduced salt concentration in the cluster, like in the bulk coacervate phase, can be attributed to the chain connectivity contribution in the electrostatic free energy, following the analysis given in ref (53). With increasing m, ϕs,c increases slightly and approaches the coacervate concentration at coexistence ϕsII in the limit of m → ∞. Notably, we observe an enrichment of salt in the surface layer of polyion cluster, but the peak value is roughly independent of m. Moreover, the salt enrichment in the interfacial layer becomes weaker with increasing ϕs,r (see Figure S2b). This behavior is qualitatively consistent with that for the planar interface as reported in our previous work, (82) and presumably arises from the chain conformational entropy at the interface. Similar to the salt-free case, quantitate study on the m-dependence of ϕp,c and ϕs,c, as shown by Figure S3, reveals that ϕp,c = ϕpII (1 + Dpm–1/3) and ϕs,c = ϕsII (1 – Dsm–1/3) at large m, where Dp >0 and Ds >0 are constants that increase with ϕs,r.
      From the structure of an m-cluster, we then calculate the free energy Wm, from which we identify the surface of the interface R* and the interfacial tension γm following eqs 10, 14, and 15. The m-dependence of these quantities is qualitatively similar to that for the salt-free cases; here, we only present γm for demonstration. In Figure 6a, we show γm as a function of m–1/3 for three values of the reservoir concentration ϕs,r. Again, we see that γm = γ∞(1 + Dγm–1/3) for large m where the slope Dγ > 0 increases with the salt reservoir concentration ϕs,r. This behavior also indicates that the interfacial tension of finite-sized cluster increases on decreasing the cluster size, and the leading correction is inversely proportional to the radius.

      III.II.II. Formation Free Energy of Clusters, Binodal, and Spinodal

      Next, we analyze the m-dependence of the cluster formation free energy ΔWm = Wm – mW1 at various salt reservoir concentrations ϕs,r. From the results shown in Figure 6b, we observe qualitatively similar behaviors to the salt-free case. Quantitatively, the magnitude of ΔWm decreases with increasing ϕs,r, reflecting the weakening of the driving force for coalescence with increasing salt. Following the same strategy as in the salt-free case, we calculate the polycation concentration in the m-clusters, ϕm, and the total polycation concentration on the supernatant binodal, ϕpI; the results are shown in Figure 7a. Again, from the overlap between the black solid curve and the red dashed curve, we see that the contribution in the supernatant phase is dominated by the contribution from polyion pairs instead of larger clusters.
      From Figure 5b, we see that the salt concentration inside the finite-sized cluster in the supernatant phase is slightly less than the salt concentration outside (the reservoir concentration) ϕs,r. However, because the concentration of clusters in the supernatant phase is quite low, to a good approximation the salt concentration in the supernatant phase is the same as that in the reservoir, i.e., ϕsI ≈ ϕs,r. By collecting ϕpII, ϕsII, ϕpI and ϕsI, we can construct the binodal in the polymer–salt concentration (i.e., ϕp–ϕs) plane.
      In Figure 7b, we show the binodal (the red solid curve). Similar to the salt-free case, we also sketch the missing part of the binodal close to the critical point, as shown by the red dotted curve, for a visual completeness of the phase diagram. For comparison, we include the binodal from the uniform mixing approximation (i.e., the black dotted curve), which is obtained by numerically solving the phase equilibrium equations (i.e., the equality of osmotic pressure, of the chemical potential of polyions, and small ions in the two coexisting phases) based on the Helmholtz free energy density given by eq 5. We note that the binodal reported in most of the previous theoretical studies is usually obtained under the uniform mixing approximation. Similar to the ϕp–lB phase diagram for the salt-free case (i.e., Figure 3a), we find that the coacervate branch obtained from both methods is nearly the same, but the polyion concentration in the dilute branch in the cluster method is several orders of magnitude larger than that from the uniform mixing approximation. The magnitude of the polyion concentration in the supernatant branch of the binodal is in the experimentally observable range over a wide range of salt concentrations. This feature is qualitatively consistent with several experimental phase diagrams. (33,49,60) Moreover, we expect the critical salt concentration in the method to be lower than predicted from the uniform mixing approximation (the black circle in Figure 7b). Finally, in the cluster treatment, the salt concentration in the supernatant phase is slightly higher than that in the coacervate phase over a wide range of salt concentrations (not shown); this behavior is similar to the salt partitioning obtained under the uniform mixing approximation. We note that it is possible to produce the opposite salt partition behavior when a specific polymer–salt attraction is included. (62,75,137)
      Using the same procedure described in the salt-free case, we also construct the pseudo-spinodal in the ϕp–ϕs plane to mark the effective limit of the metastable region; this is shown as the blue dashed-dotted curve in Figure 7b. For comparison, we also include the spinodal curve under the uniform mixing approximation (the green dotted curve), determined by the vanishing of the determinant of the Hessian matrix for the free energy density given by eq 5. We see that the pseudo-spinodal is in general larger than the uniform mixing spinodal. Based on the binodal and pseudo-spinodal in Figure 7b, we expect two types of phase separation kinetics depending on the initial polymer concentration ϕp. When ϕp is small (i.e., 5 × 10–9 ≲ ϕp ≲ 1.3 × 10–4, bracketed by the starting points of the red solid and the blue dashed-dotted curve on the horizontal axis), phase separation proceeds via the nucleation and growth kinetics under all salt concentrations ϕs,r. On the other hand, when ϕp ≳ 1.3 × 10–4, the phase separation mechanism is spinodal decomposition kinetics at low salt concentrations and changes over to nucleation and growth kinetics at increased salt concentrations.

      IV. Summary

      ARTICLE SECTIONS
      Jump To
      In this work, using our recently developed mean-field theory for inhomogeneous polyelectrolyte solutions, (82) we have examined the structure, interfacial tension, and formation free energy of symmetric finite-sized clusters in dilute solutions of oppositely charged polyions. These cluster properties are then used in combination with a simple thermodynamic theory for dilute solutions of clusters to examine their effects on the phase diagram. We find that the clusters in general consist of a uniform core and a diffusive interfacial layer. The polycation (or polyanion) concentration in the uniform core of a cluster having m polyion pairs, denoted by ϕp,c, decreases with increasing m and follows ϕp,c = ϕpII (1 + Cpm–1/3) at large m, where ϕpII is the polycation concentration in the coacervate phase and Cp >0 is a constant that increases with decreasing lB/σ or increasing ϕs,r; this is a reflection of the Laplace pressure effect. Likewise, the interfacial tension of a finite-sized cluster, γm, decreases on increasing the cluster size and follows a similar scaling relation. Furthermore, for solutions with finite ϕs,r, the small ions can be enriched in the interfacial regions of the droplet, and the strength of this enrichment decreases with increasing ϕs,r.
      Accounting for polyion pairs and clusters is shown to drastically affect the dilute branch of the phase diagram for symmetric polyelectrolyte complex coacervation. We construct the binodal and pseudo-spinodal in the ϕp–lB plane for the salt-free solutions and in the ϕp–ϕs plane for solutions with salt. While the coacervate branch of the binodal using the current approach is almost the same as that obtained under the uniform mixing approximation, the polyion concentration in the supernatant branch from the method is several orders of magnitude higher than that from the uniform mixing approximation. These behaviors are qualitatively consistent with the field-theoretical results by Delaney and Fredrickson. (43) Based on the formation free energy, we further examine the nucleation free energy of a cluster from polyion pairs in a supersaturated solution as a function of the cluster size m and identify the nucleation free energy barrier ΔG* and the critical nucleus size m*. Setting this free energy barrier to order 10 kBT allows us to obtain the pseudo-spinodal for the dilute solution. This pseudo-spinodal is shown to be also shifted significantly to higher polyion concentrations in comparison to the mean-field spinodal from the uniform mixing approximation, for both the salt-free solutions and the solutions with salt.
      Making the volume approximation for the clusters, we also provide simple analytical expressions for the cluster formation free energy, the supernatant binodal, and the nucleation barrier. In particular, we propose a simple approximate expression for the polyion concentration in the coexisting supernatant phase, ϕpI, in terms of the concentration of the coacervate phase, ϕpII, and the interfacial tension for the planer interface γ∞, in the form of kBT ln ϕpI ≈ −(36π)1/3 (Nv/ϕpII)2/3γ∞. This relation can be used as a useful order-of-magnitude estimate of ϕpI using the more easily measurable properties ϕpII and γ∞. Similarly, we are able to obtain simple expressions for the nucleation barrier ΔG* and the size of the critical nucleus m* in terms of the supersaturation S ≡ ϕ1/ϕpI, chain length N, interfacial tension γ∞, and polyion concentration in the coacervate phase ϕpII.
      By focusing on the supernatant phase, this study serves to provide a more complete picture on the global phase behavior of symmetric complex coacervation. On the other hand, the supernatant phase for asymmetric complex coacervation remains largely unexplored. Depending on the specific asymmetry conditions, the supernatant phase in equilibrium with an asymmetric coacervate may consist of finite-sized clusters as well as uncomplex polyions. In particular, the charge balance between polycation and polyanion can be violated inside the cluster, and correspondingly, the cluster usually carries a finite charge. When the amount of the finite charge is sufficiently high, the cluster may deviate from the spherical shape and adopt cylindrical or tadpole structures, as proposed by Oskolkov and Potemkin (113) and by Zhang and Shklovskii, (112) respectively. A systematic investigation of the structure of such finite-sized clusters and their influence on the binodal and phase-transition kinetics for asymmetric complex coacervation represents an interesting future direction.
